1. Realized portfolio value

Three books that all start at the same dollar: the curated one, a buy-and-hold of the starter_watchlist (AAPL, GOOGL, AMZN) bought equal-dollar on this book's FIRST day and never touched, and SPY. The control is the SAME basket on every page — it is what the curated book is measured against, not what the book starts holding, so it does not follow the seed. Squares mark the rebalances — dark red where an event actually opened or closed, orange where the curator rebalanced but changed nothing. Over this window the curated book ended at $366,973, the starter basket at $105,735, SPY at $90,975 — curating beat the starter basket and SPY. Kept OUT of the headline on purpose: a backtest steered by returns on known history is how you overfit, which is why this page leads with breadth and precision.

2. Fractional value change per curation

The book’s percent change from one curation to the next. Markers are green when the period made money, red when it lost. The panel above is cumulative and on a log axis; this is the same book read one period at a time. Across the 35 periods the median is +5.6% and the mean +6.3% ± 2.0% (standard error); the dashed line is the median. The first curation has no predecessor so it is not plotted.

3. Watchlist composition over time

One row per ticker. The pale bar is the span the curator kept it WATCHLISTED — it held the thesis; the solid bar is the span the optimizer actually FUNDED it. The gap between them is the honest part: a name the curator believed in and the math never backed. Colour is the ticker’s dominant BEAT — which part of the firehose its evidence came from. Grey means no beat-attributable evidence.

4. Event timeline

The 157 events that RAN. The pale bar spans proposed → terminated; the solid overlay is when the optimizer actually FUNDED it, coloured by beat. A bar with no solid section is a thesis the curator held and the math never backed. Two classes are not drawn, and both are counted in panel 5: 5 events with no agent read at all, and 155 that opened and terminated on the SAME curation — those draw as hairlines indistinguishable from the axis and would bury the theses that ran.

5. Live events vs the cap

Theses the curator tracked at once, split by whether the optimizer put capital behind them, against the max_events ceiling (dashed). The stack’s top edge is the live count — where it touches the dashed line the cap is binding and the lowest coverage-ranked event was retired to make room, so the knob rather than the news set what got tracked. The amber band is the allocation bottleneck: live theses the math never backed, and across the run 252 of 312 events with an agent read died never funded. The dotted line is a flow, not part of the stack — events opened and closed in a single curation, dropped from panel 4 as hairlines. Ticker counts live in the panel directly below — this panel counts THESES.

6. Breadth over time

The COUNTS behind the panel above, per rebalance: events live, tickers with a live thesis, every ticker named by a live event, and the distinct catalysts. per rebalance. Catalysts are drawn separately because several events on one theme is concentration wearing a diversity costume. The dashed line is max_watchlist = 6, which binds in 36 of 37 months, and the green line is what actually held capital. The axis is log because the series span 1 to 194.

7. Cumulative $ gain per holding

The 16 best and 8 worst funded names. Every other funded name is left OFF the chart and stated here instead: 26 more winners worth $81,676 and 15 more losers worth $30,785. They were drawn as two grey bars and are not any more — both were taller than most named tickers, so they set the y-range and squashed the comparison this panel is for. Bold tickers are the seven shortlist names — the big multi-year risers whose press named dated catalysts, i.e. the ones this strategy most wants to be holding. A result resting on one or two names is a different thing from the same return spread across many — and the difference is not visible in the equity curve above. Click any named bar for that ticker’s price history, with ▲/▼ marking the moments the optimizer funded and unfunded it.

8. Cumulative $ gain per beat

The same dollars as the panel above, rolled up to the BEAT that surfaced each ticker’s evidence — i.e. which part of the firehose paid. A beat that costs money is a retrieval-vocabulary problem, not a curator one.

9. Gain per article read, by beat

The same dollars divided by how many of that beat's articles actually REACHED THE SCOUT — i.e. survived the discovery gate. That is the cost that binds: the scout is 91% of the LLM bill and reads only gate-passed articles. The corpus count and the pass rate are in the hover. They diverge sharply — the momentum beat passes at 31% against 3-8% elsewhere, because its atoms ARE the gate's vocabulary, so it is 17% of the corpus but 35% of everything the scout reads. Beats that retrieved articles but never produced a funded position sit at zero: they are pure cost. Read it against panel 8 — a tall bar there with a short bar here is a beat carried by volume rather than by quality.

10. Cumulative $ gain per event

The same gains grouped by the EVENT that motivated them. PWR groups this by wave bucket; GHR's unit of thesis is the event, so this is its analogue. It answers whether the curator's ideas paid, independently of which vehicle expressed them.

11. Portfolio value by event over time

How the book was distributed across events as the year ran. Wide bands that persist mean concentrated conviction; a churn of thin bands means the optimizer kept rotating.

Two non-event bands. Grey is the real always_include anchors (SPY, BIL). Amber is money still funded after every event naming that ticker had terminated — the same dollars panel 10 buckets as (unassigned). Until 2026-08-22 the two were drawn as one band labelled “anchors”. The 17.3%-vs-8.1% disagreement once reported here was not a disagreement at all: this panel attributed dollars off a vehicle list TRUNCATED TO 6 for the timeline’s row labels, so every ticker past the sixth fell into the amber band. Measured on the full list, amber is 0.0% of the backtest book and 2.9% of the bootstrap’s.

Only the 8 largest events by peak holding are named in the legend — about 70 hold dollars at some point, and that many swatches cannot be matched to bands by eye. Hover any band to identify it; every event is hoverable, labelled or not.

12. Allocation over time

Dollars held per ticker, stacked — the top edge is the portfolio value. The always_include anchors (SPY, BIL) sit outside the watchlist cap and are where idle capital parks; a grey anchor stretch is the book in SPY/BIL, not a decision to hold cash. The weights sum to 1 on every day, so the book is never actually in cash.

13. Thesis concentration

How much of the whole portfolio is riding on one event. Anchors are not a bet, so a day parked in SPY/BIL reads 0%; the dashed line is the per-ticker cap, for scale.

14. Curator funnel

Everything the curator touched, from the articles it read down to the picks it logged. Log x-axis. Two things to watch: the discovery gate is the largest cut in the whole pipeline (~19×), and it is scout-only — event agents still read the full window, so tracking an event is never starved.

Units change mid-funnel: admissions counts ticker-curations, so a ticker re-admitted in a later curation is counted again; distinct tickers and events are the de-duplicated views. NOT shown: the ticker guard, which resolves names to symbols and drops unresolvable ones before these counters see them.

15. Scout inflow vs admissions

Candidate tickers the scout proposed each rebalance_period (30 days here), against what was admitted. Each candidate is a (ticker, thesis) pair, not an event — several can collapse into one event later (176 admissions became 317 events).

16. Does a bigger bundle make the scout act?

The design’s central claim, tested. Articles are bundled by company so a ticker’s move-signal and its DRIVER arrive together — a move with no cause is correctly refused, which is why RKLB produced nothing for so long. If that is right, bigger bundles should propose more often. Bars are how many bundles the scout was shown at each size; the line is the share that produced a proposal. Watch the 1-article bar: a bundle of one cannot corroborate anything, so it is the control.

17. Gains per bundle

The same dollars as the panel above, by bundle NAME rather than by size — which bundles actually paid. A bundle is credited with the realised P&L of every ticker proposed out of it, so a name here earned its money by putting a ticker in front of the scout at the right moment. The 30 largest by absolute value are drawn, winners and losers both; hover for the tickers each produced. Everything else is stated rather than drawn: 18 more bundles worth $36,388 and 15 more worth −$28,747. Rolled into bars they would be taller than the largest named bundle and would flatten everything here, the same way they did in panel 7. A ticker proposed from two bundles is credited to both, so the bars total ~107% of the book — measured 12.3% double-counted, of which COPX alone is $21,445; over DISTINCT tickers the panel covers 95.1% of realised P&L.

18. Coverage vs picks, per ticker

Article counts for the 40 most-covered tickers in the corpus. Green got watchlisted at some point; grey was named in the news but never watchlisted.

19. Gain per article, per ticker

For the picked tickers above: dollars earned per article the press wrote about them. The per-ticker twin of panel 9. A name that paid a lot on little coverage sits far right; a heavily-covered loser sits far left. Only tickers that were both in the top-40 by coverage AND funded appear, so this is a subset of the bars above.

20. Gain per lede provenance

Dollars earned, split by where the text behind each pick came from. The money twin of the panel below: that one counts ARTICLES the curator cited, this one counts what those picks actually paid. Each ticker’s P&L is divided across the provenance of its own evidence in proportion — a pick argued off six archived articles and two live pages contributes 75%/25%, since neither can be said to have caused it. Read against the panel below: if archived supplies most of the reading but live page most of the money, the quotable arm is not the one earning.

21. Evidence by lede provenance

For every article the curator cited as evidence, where its text came from. If picks cluster on archived text (Wayback, look-ahead-clean) the clean arm is earning its cost; if they cluster on live page text the corpus is leaning on look-ahead-biased material.

22. Evidence by source

Which outlets actually produced the articles behind the picks. Compare with the firehose dashboard's source panel: an outlet supplying much of the corpus but little of the evidence is volume without signal.

23. Evidence by beat

Which standing searches (retrieval_config.json) produced the articles behind the picks. A beat that fills the corpus but never appears here is paying rent without earning it.

24. Event storyboard

Each event's week-by-week journal: what the agent concluded, and why it eventually exited. The qualitative counterpart to the curation log — the only place you can see whether the exit logic is REASONING about a catalyst resolving or just pattern-matching on a price move. Funded events first, then those that never held capital.

            25. Text provenance of what the curator read

            Per week, how much of the pool reached the curator as archived text, live-page text, a search snippet, or a bare headline. This is the firehose's provenance panel restricted to the slices the curator actually read. Archived = Wayback (archive.org's snapshot as of the article's own date), which is the only look-ahead-CLEAN text here: a live page is fetched today and may have been edited, extended or corrected since publication, so it can carry knowledge the curator could not have had. A week leaning on live text is a week whose result is an upper bound. Search snippet is the text the retrieval engine itself returned — the only text a websearch article ever has — captured at PULL time, which for the daily forward pull is within ~24h of publication, so it is cleaner than a live fetch without being an archive. Until 2026-08-26 this class did not exist and those snippets were OVERWRITTEN BY THE TITLE before the curator read them, which is why every pre-2026-08-26 curation shows the post-handoff era as headline-only: the chart was right, the pipeline was throwing the text away.

An event is one catalyst and the basket of tickers expressing it, so opening an event is GHR's analogue of an add. Proposed→admitted is what the scout put forward versus what survived the inflow cap, so a week where those differ is a week the cap bound.
